title: The Morrigan: The Great Queen
summary: A month with the Morrigan, Ireland’s Great Queen of battle, prophecy and sovereignty: her names and sisters, her stories by the river and the ford, how little we know of her worship, and how people honour her now, ending in a self-dedication made with your word.
welcome:
This journey takes about a lunar month. You will read five lessons, set up a shrine, keep nine nights of offering and truth-telling, and decide with care whether to dedicate yourself to the Morrigan.

It is a self-dedication, not an initiation, and it does not make you a member of any priesthood or group. The Morrigan is a goddess of war and death as well as sovereignty, and these lessons are honest about her fierce side. The practices here are devotional and protective only; nothing in this journey curses or harms anyone. You can pause at any point and the journey will wait.
about: The Morrigan (Old Irish Mór-Ríoghain or Morrígan, often translated “Great Queen”, though it may mean “Phantom Queen”) appears in medieval Irish tales as a shape-shifting goddess of battle, prophecy, fate and sovereignty. She is sometimes one figure and sometimes one of three sisters, named in different sources as Badb (crow), Macha and Nemain or Anand. She mates with the Dagda at Samhain by a river and promises him victory, she rouses and tests Cú Chulainn, she flies over battles as a crow, and after the Battle of Mag Tuired she proclaims peace to all Ireland. Almost nothing survives of how she was worshipped: no temple, no prayer, and only a handful of places named for her. Today she has one of the largest devotional followings of any Irish deity, among Celtic polytheists, Pagans, witches and some veterans, and her devotees tend to stress courage, truth, keeping your word and service rather than aesthetics.
notes: The evidence for the Morrigan is literary: medieval Irish tales and glosses written by Christian monks. There is no surviving record of her cult, rites or priesthood. Modern devotion fills a large gap, and the lessons say so.
She is not a "triple goddess" of maiden, mother and crone. Her three-ness comes from Irish sisters and names, and the lists differ from text to text.
She is not Morgan le Fay of Arthurian legend. The names look alike but come from different roots and traditions.

This journey is devotional and defensive only. It describes the Morrigan’s war and death imagery honestly, but it includes no curses, binding of others or harmful work, and it asks you not to use her name for revenge.
Do not promise her anything you cannot do. Devotees of every kind agree that a broken promise is worse than none. Make small vows and keep them.
If you live with trauma from violence or war, go gently. Her imagery can stir hard memories; a counsellor, veterans’ service or trusted friend is a better first support than any rite.

stages.title: At the ford
stages.intro: Begin by making a plain place for the Morrigan and introducing yourself honestly. In the stories she meets people at fords and rivers, the crossing places. This is your first crossing: say who you are, and listen.

practices.title: Set up a simple shrine
practices.instructions: Choose a shelf or small table where you will not be disturbed. Lay down a dark cloth, black, red or deep green. Place a candle in a sturdy holder on a heatproof dish, a small cup or glass for offerings of drink, and a bowl of water to stand for the river where she washes. Add one image of a crow or raven (a photograph or postcard is fine; you do not need a skull or feathers), and one object that stands for something you defend or are responsible for: a family photograph, your work badge, a key to your home. Keep it uncluttered. Many of her devotees say she prefers an honest shrine to a dramatic one.
practices.prompt: What did you put on her shrine to stand for what you protect? Why that?

rite.title: Introduction to the Morrigan
rite.summary: A short, honest rite of introduction: light a flame, pour water as the river, give a drink and bread, say who you are and what you are responsible for, and listen.

ingredients.name: A black or red candle in a safe holder
A small glass of red wine, whiskey or milk (or blackcurrant juice)
A piece of bread or an oatcake

rite.preparation: Wash your hands and face. Turn off your phone. Spend a few minutes writing down, plainly, who you are and what you are responsible for: people, work, causes, your own body and life. Pour the drink and set the bread on a plate before the shrine.

steps.title: Stand at the river
steps.instructions: Stand before the shrine. Put both hands in the bowl of water and hold them there for a few breaths, as though standing at a ford. Then lift them out and let the water drip back.
steps.spoken: Great Queen, I come to the ford. I come with my hands open.

steps.title: Light the flame
steps.spoken: Morrigan, Great Queen, I light this flame in your honour.

steps.title: Give the offering
steps.instructions: Lift the cup and the bread, then set them down before the candle.
steps.spoken: Here is drink and bread, freely given. I ask nothing in return tonight.

steps.title: Say who you are
steps.instructions: Read aloud what you wrote: your name, your life, what you are responsible for and what you defend. Do not dress it up. If something on the list is a struggle or a failure, say so.

steps.title: Listen
steps.instructions: Sit in silence with the flame. Do not look for signs; just notice what you feel and think. If nothing comes, that is fine and very normal.

steps.title: Close
steps.instructions: Thank her and snuff the candle.
steps.spoken: Great Queen, thank you for hearing me. I will come again, and I will keep my word.

rite.closing: Leave the offering for a few hours or overnight. Then pour the drink onto the earth outside (not where pets can reach it), and put the bread out for the birds, crumbled small, or in the compost. Write a few lines about how the rite felt.
rite.safety: Keep the candle on a heatproof dish and never leave it unattended. Alcohol poured outside should go away from pets and children; grapes, raisins and alcohol are toxic to dogs and cats, so use blackcurrant juice or milk if you have animals at home.

stages.title: Learning who she is
stages.intro: Four lessons on the Morrigan: her names and sisters, her stories, what we know (and don’t) about her worship, and how people honour her today. Read one every day or two.

lessons.title: Many names: Morrigan, Badb, Macha, Nemain, Anand
lessons.summary: What her name means, who her sisters are, how her three-ness works in Irish texts, and what she is not.

sections.heading: What “Morrigan” means
sections.body:
In the oldest Irish texts her name is Morrígan; later writers spell it Mór-Ríoghain, “Great Queen”, and that is the meaning most devotees use. Many scholars think the first part is not mór, “great”, but mor, an old word linked to nightmare (the same root as the “mare” in English nightmare), which would make her the “Phantom Queen”. Both readings are defended. It is fair to call her either, and fair to say we do not know which the earliest storytellers meant.

She is one of the Tuatha Dé Danann, the divine people of Irish myth, and in the medieval Book of Invasions (Lebor Gabála Érenn) she is one of the daughters of a woman called Ernmas.

sections.heading: The sisters
sections.body:
The Book of Invasions names three daughters of Ernmas: Badb, Macha, and the Morrigan, “whose name was Anand”. Other texts group the Morrigan with Badb and Nemain, or treat “the Morrigan” as a title any of them could carry. Lady Gregory, retelling the tales in 1904, lists them among the great women of the Tuatha Dé: “Badb, a battle goddess; and Macha, whose mast-feeding was the heads of men killed in battle; and the Morrigu, the Crow of Battle.”

Badb means crow, specifically the hooded or scald crow that gathers after battle; she is often Badb Catha, “battle crow”. Nemain means something like frenzy or panic, the terror that runs through an army. Macha gives her name to Emain Macha, the royal seat of Ulster near Armagh; one Macha is a woman forced to race the king’s horses while pregnant, who curses the men of Ulster with weakness in their time of need. Anand or Anu is called in Cormac’s Glossary the mother of the gods of Ireland, and two hills in Kerry, the Paps of Anu, are named after her.

sections.heading: Three, but not maiden, mother, crone
sections.body:
Irish storytellers loved threes: three sisters, three blows, three drops, three Brigits. The Morrigan’s three-ness is part of this. It is not the maiden, mother and crone of modern Wicca, a pattern popularised by Robert Graves in the twentieth century. None of the Morrigan’s sisters is a maiden or a crone in that sense.

Some devotees honour the Morrigan as one goddess with many names; some honour Badb, Macha and the Morrigan as distinct goddesses who sometimes act together; some honour Macha or Badb alone. The texts support all three readings in different places. What matters in practice is to be clear in your own prayers about whom you are addressing.

sections.heading: Outside Ireland, and what she is not
sections.body:
There is one intriguing piece of evidence from Gaul. A worn Roman-period altar found in 1867 near Mieussy in the French Alps was set up by a woman named Servilia Terentia to a goddess whose name survives as [.]ATHUBODUA. Most scholars restore the lost first letter to read Cathubodua, “battle crow”, the same name as the Irish Badb Catha. If that is right, a battle-crow goddess was known among Celtic-speaking peoples well beyond Ireland, but it rests on a single damaged stone and a restored letter.

The Morrigan is often confused with Morgan le Fay, the enchantress of Arthurian romance. The names sound alike, but Morgan comes from a Welsh or Breton root linked with the sea, and the two figures belong to different literatures. She is also sometimes identified with the banshee (bean sí) of later folklore, who keens before a death in certain families. The two are related ideas, but the banshee is a folk figure, not the same goddess.

knowAndDont.known: Medieval Irish texts name the Morrigan with sisters Badb and Macha, and in some texts Nemain; one says her name was Anand. Badb means crow. An altar from Mieussy in Gaul names a goddess usually read as Cathubodua, “battle crow”. Cormac’s Glossary calls Anu the mother of the Irish gods.
knowAndDont.unknown: We do not know whether these were originally one goddess, several, or a title; the texts disagree. The meaning of the name (Great Queen or Phantom Queen) is debated. The link between the Irish Badb and the Gaulish Cathubodua rests on one inscription, whose first letter has to be restored.

lessons.inPractice: Devotees address her as the Morrigan, the Great Queen, or Mór-Ríoghain, and sometimes Badb or Macha separately. Many groups, such as the US-based Coru Cathubodua Priesthood, take names from the Gaulish inscription. Some people keep separate days or offerings for each sister.
reflect: Which of her names catches you most: Great Queen, Phantom Queen, battle crow, frenzy, mother of the gods? Why?
Have you been carrying a picture of her that is closer to modern imagery than to the texts? What is it?
further: Angelique Gulermovich Epstein, War Goddess: The Morrígan and Her Germano-Celtic Counterparts (PhD dissertation, UCLA, 1998).
Morgan Daimler, Pagan Portals: The Morrigan: Meeting the Great Queens (Moon Books, 2014), a short, careful introduction by a Gaelic polytheist.
Lebor Gabála Érenn, ed. R. A. S. Macalister, Irish Texts Society (1938–56).

lessons.title: By the river and at the ford: her stories
lessons.summary: The Samhain meeting with the Dagda, her prophecy of peace, her testing of Cú Chulainn, and what these tales say about sovereignty and fate.

sections.heading: The river at Samhain
sections.body:
The great tale of the Morrigan is in Cath Maige Tuired, the Second Battle of Mag Tuired. Before the battle between the Tuatha Dé and the Fomorians, at Samhain, the Dagda goes to meet her at a river in Connacht, the Unshin near Corann in County Sligo. Lady Gregory’s retelling of the Dagda’s journey puts it this way: “he saw the Battle-Crow, the Morrigu, washing herself in the river Unius of Connacht, and one of her two feet at Ullad Echne, to the south of the water, and the other at Loscuinn, to the north of the water, and her hair hanging in nine loosened locks.”

Gregory leaves out what follows; the medieval text says they lie together, and the place was afterwards called the Bed of the Couple. She promises the Dagda that she will take the heart’s blood of the Fomorian king Indech for the Tuatha Dé. It is a story of union between a war goddess and the father-god on the night the year turns, and devotees today often keep Samhain in her honour because of it.

sections.heading: Peace up to the skies
sections.body:
When the battle is won, the Morrigan proclaims the victory to the royal hills, the rivers and the river-mouths of Ireland. In Gregory’s words: “Peace up to the skies, the skies down to earth, the earth under the skies; strength to every one.” It is easy to forget that the war goddess is the one who announces peace.

The medieval text then gives her a second prophecy, darker: a vision of the end of the world, when summers will be without flowers, cattle without milk, women without modesty and men without courage, judges will be unjust and every man a betrayer. She sees both the peace that is won and the decay that comes when people forget their duties. Her prophecy is not a curse; it is a warning about what people do to each other.

sections.heading: The Morrigan and Cú Chulainn
sections.body:
In the Ulster tales she meets the hero Cú Chulainn several times. In one she wakes him from an enchanted sleep with a taunt, which Gregory renders: “There is not the making of a hero in you,” she said to him, “and you lying there under the feet of shadows.” He gets up and fights. In another she drives a cow past him and they quarrel; she tells him she guards his death.

In the Táin Bó Cúailnge she comes to him as a young woman offering her love and help, and he rudely refuses. She attacks him during his single combats as an eel, a she-wolf and a red heifer, and he wounds her each time. Afterwards she appears as an old woman milking a three-teated cow, and he, not knowing her, asks for milk; with each drink he blesses her and she is healed. In the later tale of his death, a crow, the Badb, settles on his shoulder as he dies standing, tied to a pillar.

sections.heading: What the stories are about
sections.body:
Read together, these tales are about sovereignty, the right relationship between a ruler, a people and the land. The Morrigan chooses whom she will help. She offers, tests and warns. She can be refused, but refusing her has consequences. She brings fear (Nemain) and also fury, rousing a hero to stand up. She knows how things will end and says so plainly.

This is why modern devotees emphasise courage, honesty and keeping one’s word. She is not a goddess of random slaughter. In the tales, she is drawn to the moment when a person, a king or a people must decide who they are and act on it.

knowAndDont.known: Cath Maige Tuired tells of her Samhain union with the Dagda at the Unshin and her two prophecies after the battle. The Ulster cycle, especially the Táin Bó Cúailnge and the shorter Táin Bó Regamna, tells of her encounters with Cú Chulainn. The place-name lore (Dindshenchas) adds more stories, such as her turning a woman named Odras into a pool.
knowAndDont.unknown: These are literary tales written down by Christian scribes from the eighth to the twelfth centuries, drawing on older tradition we cannot see. We do not know how they related to any living worship. Modern readings of the tales as teachings about sovereignty and courage are interpretation.

lessons.inPractice: Many devotees read the Táin and Cath Maige Tuired as sacred stories and return to them regularly. Some keep a Samhain vigil for the Dagda’s meeting with her, and some recite her peace prophecy at the end of rites.
reflect: Where in your life have you been asleep “under the feet of shadows”? What would it take to stand up?
Cú Chulainn refuses her and is wounded; later he blesses her without knowing her and she is healed. What do you make of that?
further: Lady Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Part I Book II ch. III, “The Great Battle of Magh Tuireadh”, and Book IV ch. IV, “The Morrigu” (public domain, Project Gutenberg).
The Táin, trans. Thomas Kinsella (1969) or Ciaran Carson (2007).
Cath Maige Tuired, ed. and trans. Elizabeth A. Gray (Irish Texts Society, 1982).

lessons.title: How was she worshipped? What we don’t know
lessons.summary: The thin evidence for her cult, the places named after her, and how modern devotion has had to build almost from nothing.

sections.heading: No temple, no prayer
sections.body:
It is important to be honest about this: we have no record of how anyone worshipped the Morrigan. No altar inscribed to her has been found in Ireland. No prayer, hymn or rite survives. No early writer describes priests or priestesses of hers. Everything we know comes from tales, place-names and the notes of medieval scholars.

Those scholars were monks. When one of them glossed the Latin word lamia, a female night-demon in the Book of Isaiah, he wrote “Morrigan” beside it. That tells us how a Christian scholar saw her, not how her worshippers did. When you read that the Morrigan was “a terrible demon” or “the goddess of war of the pagan Irish”, remember that both descriptions come from people looking back at her from outside.

sections.heading: Places with her name
sections.body:
A few places carry her name or her stories. At Rathcroghan in County Roscommon, the ancient royal site of Connacht, a narrow cave called Oweynagat (Uaimh na gCat, the Cave of the Cats) is usually identified with the síd (otherworld mound) of Cruachan, from which, in Táin Bó Regamna, she drives a cow. The cave can be visited on guided tours from the Rathcroghan Visitor Centre. It is wet, narrow and protected; never go in alone or without permission.

At Brú na Bóinne, the Newgrange complex, the medieval lists of wonders at the Dagda’s house include a Hall of the Morrigan, and modern writers also point to two mounds there called the Paps of the Morrigan, though that identification is less secure. Cath Maige Tuired names a Bed of the Couple by the Unshin. The Paps of Anu in Kerry are two rounded hills topped with cairns, named for Anu, who is sometimes identified with the Morrigan. None of these sites has produced evidence of her cult; they are places where her stories were told.

sections.heading: Echoes in folklore
sections.body:
Later Irish and Scottish folklore has figures who feel related: the washer at the ford, a woman seen washing the clothes or armour of those about to die (in Scotland the bean nighe); the banshee who keens before a death; the hooded crow, feared as a bird that picks at the dying. The medieval tale of the Destruction of Da Derga’s Hostel has a woman like Badb at the door, foretelling ruin.

These are echoes, not proof of continuous worship. They show that the idea of a female figure who knows death and warns of it remained alive in Gaelic culture for a very long time.

sections.heading: Building honestly
sections.body:
Modern devotion to the Morrigan is a revival, and the honest practitioner says so. People build their practice from the tales, from what is known of early Irish religion more generally (offerings at water, gatherings at the quarter days, the importance of honour and hospitality), from the folklore, and from their own experience of her.

This is not a weakness if it is named. The problems come when modern ideas are presented as ancient facts: that she demanded blood sacrifice, that she had a specific moon phase, that a certain crystal is “hers” by tradition. Correspondences like obsidian or garnet are modern choices. Use them if they help you, but call them yours.

knowAndDont.known: There is no surviving evidence of the Morrigan’s cult in Ireland. Medieval glossators equated her with the lamia. Oweynagat at Rathcroghan, the Paps of Anu and the Hall of the Morrigan at Brú na Bóinne are linked with her in medieval lore.
knowAndDont.unknown: We do not know whether she had priests, shrines, festivals or offerings, or whether the tales reflect a goddess actually worshipped or a literary figure. Modern correspondences (colours, crystals, herbs) and modern rites are reconstructions or personal practice.

lessons.inPractice: Some devotees make pilgrimages to Rathcroghan or the Paps of Anu, often in organised groups and with respect for local landowners and the heritage sites. Most practise at home, building from the tales and keeping careful notes of what they do and why.
reflect: How do you feel about honouring a goddess whose worship has to be largely rebuilt? Is it freeing, unsettling, or both?
Which of your current ideas about her came from a book, a website or social media rather than the tales? Write them down and look at them honestly.
further: Ronald Hutton, Pagan Britain (2013), on the limits of evidence for Celtic religion.
Rathcroghan Visitor Centre, Tulsk, Co. Roscommon: rathcroghan.ie, for guided visits to Oweynagat.

lessons.title: Devotion today: courage, truth and service
lessons.summary: Who honours the Morrigan now, what they do, and how to approach a fierce goddess without romanticising war or using her for revenge.

sections.heading: Who honours her
sections.body:
The Morrigan has a large and active modern following. Celtic Reconstructionists and Gaelic polytheists honour her within a reconstructed Irish practice, often learning Irish and following the old calendar. Devotional polytheists, including the Coru Cathubodua Priesthood in the United States, treat her as a real goddess to be served with discipline. Wiccans and witches honour her as a dark goddess or Samhain goddess. Some veterans, soldiers, nurses, emergency workers and activists find in her a goddess who understands their work.

These groups differ. Reconstructionists will tell you to read the Irish sources and be cautious of modern correspondences. Eclectic witches may combine her with other goddesses. Both can be sincere; it helps to know which conversation you are joining.

sections.heading: What devotees do
sections.body:
Most devotion to the Morrigan is practical. People dedicate their training, their study or their work to her. They keep promises. They speak up for those being harmed. They prepare for hard things rather than avoiding them: a difficult conversation, a medical treatment, a legal fight, a long recovery. Some feed crows and ravens as a daily offering. Some learn a martial art, a self-defence course or first aid.

Offerings are usually simple: red wine, whiskey, milk, bread, red apples or blackberries, a poem, a lit candle, and especially an act carried through to the end. Irish folklore says blackberries should not be picked after Samhain because the púca has spoiled them, so devotees gather or buy them before then.

sections.heading: Not a revenge goddess
sections.body:
Because she is a war goddess, people sometimes come to her angry and ask her to punish someone. This journey does not support that, and many experienced devotees would warn you off it too. In the tales she is a goddess of sovereignty and fate, not anyone’s hired hand. Asking her to harm others turns devotion into a transaction and usually brings grief to the person asking.

Ask instead for courage, clarity and protection. Ask for the strength to leave, to fight fairly, to tell the truth, to defend those who cannot defend themselves. If you are in danger, the most devoted thing you can do is to contact the people and services who can keep you safe.

sections.heading: Without the costume
sections.body:
Much online imagery of the Morrigan is about aesthetics: black lace, blood, skulls, ravens. There is nothing wrong with beauty, but devotees often say she cares more for what you do than how you look. War is not glamorous, and she knows that better than anyone; the battlefield crows eat the dead.

A good test is to ask, after each rite: what will I do differently tomorrow? If the answer is nothing, the rite was theatre. If the answer is that you will keep a promise you have been avoiding, you are closer to her.

knowAndDont.known: There are active modern communities devoted to the Morrigan, including Celtic Reconstructionists, Gaelic polytheists, devotional priesthoods and Wiccan and eclectic witches. Their practices are documented in their own writings and gatherings.
knowAndDont.unknown: Modern devotional practices, such as feeding crows, dedicating training or keeping vows to her, are not attested in early sources. They are thoughtful responses to the tales. Claims that she "demands" particular sacrifices or behaviour are personal experience or community teaching, not historical fact.

lessons.inPractice: A typical devotee keeps a small shrine, lights a candle on a regular day, makes offerings of drink, bread or berries, feeds the local crows, reads the Irish tales, and dedicates a discipline (exercise, study, advocacy) to her. Some join groups that hold rites at Samhain or larger gatherings.
reflect: Is there something you need courage for right now? What would it look like to dedicate that courage to her?
What draws you to her: her power, her honesty, her imagery? Be honest about which.
further: Morgan Daimler, Pagan Portals: The Morrigan: Meeting the Great Queens (2014).
Stephanie Woodfield, Celtic Lore and Spellcraft of the Dark Goddess (2011), for a Wiccan-eclectic approach.
Erynn Rowan Laurie and Kathryn Price NicDhàna et al., The CR FAQ (2007), on Celtic Reconstructionism.

practices.title: Read by her flame
practices.instructions: Before you read each lesson, light her candle and say, “Great Queen, let me see clearly.” Afterwards, write one sentence about what you will do with what you learned, then snuff the candle.
practices.prompt: One thing you learned, and one action it suggests.

practices.title: Meet the crows
practices.instructions: Once this week, go somewhere crows, rooks, ravens or jackdaws gather, and watch them for twenty minutes. Notice how they move, call, and treat one another. If you want to feed them, use unsalted peanuts, plain oats, a little cooked egg or suet pellets, not bread, and check local rules about feeding wild birds.
practices.prompt: What did you notice about the crows? What did they teach you about her?

stages.title: Nine nights of offering and truth
stages.intro: Now you put what you have learned into a nightly practice. For nine nights you give a small offering and speak one truth. The practice is simple and it is not meant to be easy; it is about steadiness and honesty, which is what her devotees prize.

lessons.title: Her days, offerings and the shape of a rite
lessons.summary: When to honour her, what to give and how, how to keep a vow, and how a simple home rite to the Morrigan runs.

sections.heading: Her days
sections.body:
The one holy day the tales give her is Samhain, the night of 31 October into 1 November, when she meets the Dagda at the river. Gaelic polytheists and Pagans alike keep it in her honour. Many devotees also mark Bealtaine, the start of summer, as the other great turning point of the year, and some keep the anniversary of a battle in Irish history, or Remembrance Day, as a time to honour the dead of war.

For regular practice, choose a day of the week and stick to it. Many people choose Tuesday, the day of Mars, which is a modern correspondence rather than an Irish one, but practical. Others honour her at the dark moon. There is no ancient rule here, so pick what you can keep.

sections.heading: Offerings, and the manner of offering
sections.body:
Give what you can afford and give it fully. Red wine, whiskey, milk, bread, oatcakes, red apples, blackberries, honey, a poem or song, and a candle lit for her all fit. So do acts: an hour of training, a donation to a veterans’ charity or a shelter, an afternoon cleaning a war memorial or a graveyard.

Set the offering before her with a clear statement of what it is. Leave it a few hours or overnight. Then give it to the earth or to the crows; do not eat or drink it yourself afterwards. Pour drink on the ground outside, not down the sink if you can avoid it, and away from places where pets or children play. If you promise an offering, give exactly what you promised, and on time.

sections.heading: Vows, and why small is better
sections.body:
Early Irish heroes lived under geasa, binding taboos or obligations; breaking a geis brought disaster, and Cú Chulainn’s death begins when he is forced to break his. Modern devotees often speak of vows to the Morrigan with the same seriousness.

The practical wisdom here is to make small vows with clear limits. “I will light your candle every Tuesday until Samhain” is a good vow. “I will serve you forever” is not, because you cannot know what forever will hold. If you find you cannot keep a vow, go before her, say so honestly, and make what amends you can. That is better than letting it quietly lapse.

sections.heading: The shape of a home rite
sections.body:
A simple rite to the Morrigan has five parts. First, prepare: wash, quiet yourself, and set out the offering. Second, call: light her candle, put your hands in the water bowl as at a ford, and address her by name. Third, give: present the offering and say what it is. Fourth, speak and listen: say what you need to say plainly, whether truth, gratitude, a request for courage, or a vow, and then sit in silence. Fifth, close: thank her, snuff the flame, and decide on one action.

That last part matters most. Her rites end with something to do. If you also want a protective working, for your home or yourself, use one that defends rather than attacks; the app’s warding working before spirit work is a good model.

knowAndDont.known: The tales place her meeting with the Dagda at Samhain. Geasa, binding obligations, appear throughout early Irish literature. Offerings at water and the importance of honour are well attested in early Irish culture generally.
knowAndDont.unknown: There is no record of specific offerings to the Morrigan, her holy days beyond the Samhain story, or the form of her rites. Weekly days, moon phases, the five-part rite shape and offering lists are modern practice.

lessons.inPractice: Many devotees keep a weekly candle, a monthly offering, and a Samhain rite. Vows are written down and reviewed. Offerings are given to the earth or the crows the next day.
reflect: What vow could you make to her that you are sure you can keep?
What would you offer if you could only offer an action, not a thing?
further: Dáithí Ó hÓgáin, The Sacred Isle: Belief and Religion in Pre-Christian Ireland (1999).
Kevin Danaher, The Year in Ireland (1972), on Samhain customs.

practices.title: Nine nights of offering and truth
practices.instructions: Each evening for nine nights, light her candle, put your hands in the water bowl, and set out a small offering: a splash of drink, a piece of bread, a few berries. Then say aloud one true thing you have been avoiding saying, even to yourself. It can be small. Sit in silence for five minutes. Before you snuff the candle, name one thing you will do tomorrow because of that truth. In the morning, give the offering to the earth or the crows, and do the thing you named.
practices.prompt: What truth did you speak tonight, and what did you do about it the next day?

stages.title: Discernment at the crossing
stages.intro: Before any dedication, stop and look at what this month has been. The Morrigan is a goddess of fate and consequence; a dedication to her is not a light thing. Stopping here, waiting a year, or choosing another god or path are all good outcomes, and nothing is failed by them.

practices.title: A sober look
practices.instructions: Read back through your journal for the whole month. Then, at her shrine with the candle lit, write honest answers to the questions below. Leave them overnight before deciding anything.
practices.prompt: Your answers to the discernment questions, and what you decided.

questions: Did you keep the nine nights? If not, what got in the way, and what does that tell you about the vow you might make?
Are you coming to her mainly for power, protection, or revenge? If revenge is part of it, can you set that down before dedicating?
Are you able to hold her war and death imagery without it harming your mental health? Is this a good season of your life for it?
Can you commit to a small, regular practice, and to telling the truth when you fall short?
Do you want a relationship with her, or with the idea of her? Both are understandable; only one needs a dedication.
Would Badb, Macha or another goddess, or a different path altogether, fit you better? Choosing them, or pausing, is a good and honest outcome.

stages.title: Dedication by your word
stages.intro: If you choose to go on, this is a self-dedication to the Morrigan: a promise you make before her, alone, in your own words. It is not an initiation into any priesthood or tradition and does not replace one where groups have their own. Many people choose Samhain eve for it; any evening when you are ready will do.

rite.title: Self-dedication to the Morrigan
rite.summary: A rite at the ford: wash your hands in her river, give a full offering, speak your vow, receive her courage, and name the first act of your dedication.

ingredients.name: A black or red candle in a safe holder
Red wine, whiskey or milk in a cup (or blackcurrant juice)
Bread or oatcakes, and red apples or blackberries
A crow or raven image, or a single found black feather
A sprig of rowan or a few rowan berries

rite.preparation: Write your vow over several days. Make it specific and limited: what you will do, how often, for how long (a year is a good span). Include one ongoing act of courage or service. Wash and dress in clean clothes. Set the shrine with the candle unlit, the water, drink, food and vow.

steps.title: Come to the ford
steps.instructions: Stand before the shrine. Put both hands in the water and hold them there.
steps.spoken: Great Queen, I come to the ford of my own free will, with clean hands and an open face.

steps.title: Light the flame
steps.instructions: Light the candle. If you have rowan, lay it beside the candle as a sign of protection for the rite.
steps.spoken: Morrigan, Mór-Ríoghain, Great Queen of the Tuatha Dé, I light this flame for you.

steps.title: Give the full offering
steps.instructions: Present the drink, the bread and the fruit one by one, naming each. Give them fully; do not take any back.
steps.spoken: This is given to you, all of it, freely.

steps.title: Speak your vow
steps.instructions: Stand. Read your vow aloud, slowly and clearly. Then say in your own words that this is a self-dedication made in good faith, that you will keep it as well as you are able, and that if you fail you will come and say so.
steps.spoken: This is my word, given to you. I will keep it, and if I fail I will come to you and say so.

steps.title: Sit in silence
steps.instructions: Sit with the flame. Ask for courage and clear sight, and then be quiet. Notice what comes and do not demand a sign.

steps.title: Name the first act
steps.instructions: Say aloud the first thing you will do as her dedicant, something you can do within the next three days.

steps.title: Proclaim peace and close
steps.instructions: As she did after the battle, end with peace. Thank her and snuff the candle.
steps.spoken: Peace up to the skies, the skies down to earth, the earth under the skies; strength to every one. Great Queen, thank you.

rite.closing: Keep your vow where you will see it. Leave the offering overnight and give it to the earth or the crows in the morning. Do your first act within three days, and write in your journal when you have.
rite.safety: Keep the candle on a heatproof dish and never leave it unattended. Keep alcohol, grapes, raisins and leftovers away from pets. If you collect a feather, leave it if you are unsure of the species: in many countries it is illegal to possess feathers of protected birds.

stages.title: Keeping your word
stages.intro: The relationship lives in kept promises. Here is a rhythm for the year: a weekly flame, offerings, Samhain, and a yearly renewal of your vow.

practices.title: Weekly flame and truth
practices.instructions: On your chosen day each week, light her candle, give a small offering, speak one truth and name one act. Feed the crows if that is part of your practice.
practices.prompt: What did you face this week, and what did you do?

practices.title: Samhain at the river
practices.instructions: At Samhain, go to a river or stream if you can, or use your water bowl at home. Tell the story of her meeting with the Dagda. Make a full offering, honour your own dead and the dead of war, and recite her proclamation of peace.
practices.prompt: What ended for you this year, and what begins?

practices.title: Yearly renewal of your vow
practices.instructions: On the anniversary of your dedication, read last year’s vow before her. Say honestly what you kept and what you did not. Write a new vow for the next year, or choose to release the vow and end the dedication with thanks. Both are honourable.
practices.prompt: What did keeping (or breaking) your word teach you this year?
